etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Contraction of 仕(し)様(よう)がない (shiyō ga nai, literally “there is no way”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English tennis court.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Short for マスコミュニケーション (masu komyunikēshon).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the classical upper bigrade verb (ラ行上二段活用) 下(お)る (oru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The adverbial -く (-ku) form of adjective 無い (nai, “not, missing, not present”) + verb なる (naru, “to become”): literally, "to become not, to become nonexistent".
The 亡 spelling of the na- root of nai and naku naru is reserved for the meaning of "dead, gone".
Cognate with 無(な)くなる (naku naru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 代(か)わる (kawaru, “to substitute”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: As above, with rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By surface analysis, 何で (“why, how”) + も.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 入(い)れる (ireru) + 物(もの) (-mono)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 可 (MC khaX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Originally meant "deeply touching or moving", without a negative connotation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 地球 (Dìqiú), coined by Matteo Ricci.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Classical Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 奨学(しょうがく) (shōgaku) + 金(きん) (-kin)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/seu/ → /ɕeu/ → /ɕoː/
From Middle Chinese 小 (MC sjewX).
The suffix sense is a clipping of 小学校 (shōgakkō, “elementary school”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ko₁/ → /ko/
From the Old Japanese stem こ (ko-). Cognate with 子 (ko, “child”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/wo/ → /o/
From the Old Japanese stem を (wo-), modern お (o-).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the Old Japanese stem ささ (sasa-), found in terms such as 笹 (sasa, “bamboo grass”), 囁く (sasayaku, “to whisper”), and 些か (isasaka, “a little”), all related to small or slight.
Saza appears to be a later derivation from sasa.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally an extension of 跡(あと) (ato, “footprint; leftover”), itself a compound of 足(あ) (a, “foot”) + 所(と) (to, “place”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 遅(おく)れる (okureru, “to be late; to be delayed; to come after something else”).
Examples appear from at least the 1300s.
More commonly spelled with the okurigana.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Uncommon alternative spelling.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/siripe/ → /çirife/ → /çirie/
From Old Japanese. Found in the Nihon Shoki of 720, and phonetically as 志利弊 (siripe₁) in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Compound of 尻 (shiri, “butt, tail, rear”) + 方 (e, “side, facing, way, direction”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Ultimate derivation unknown.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Ultimate derivation unknown. May be cognate with より (yori, “from; after”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 後 (huwX, huwH, “after”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 後 (huwX, “after”). Classified as the kan'on, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Mandarin reading hòu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 惡 (MC 'ak).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Root of the adjective 悪(わる)い (warui, “bad, evil, wicked”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/wo/ → /o/
From Middle Chinese 惡 (MC 'uH).
The 漢(かん)音(おん) (kan'on) pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/si/ → /ɕi/
Appears to be a conflation of Middle Chinese 死 (MC sijX), with an Old Japanese root that happened to have a similar pronunciation to the Middle Chinese and was probably cognate with 去る (saru, “to go, to go away”). Compare modern Mandarin 死 (sǐ).
In kanji compounds, this would be considered as on'yomi; but on its own, this could be considered as either on'yomi or kun'yomi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Related to 早(はや)い (hayai, “early, fast”) and 逸(はや)る (hayaru, “to be impatient”), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *paya.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 番(ばん) (ban, “turn”) + 組(ぐ)み (-gumi, “set (of items)”). The kumi changes to gumi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Literally, “deviance from normalcy.”

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 癌.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from verb 割る (waru, “to split, to break, to crack”), as imperfect form wara- + auxiliary verb ふ (fu, indicating repetition or ongoing state: modern verb ending う u): "to be in the act of cracking up / breaking open".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ito.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the negative continuative form of the verb 絶える (taeru, “to cease”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨mo₂no₂⟩ → /mono/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720. Theorized to derive from Proto-Japonic *mənə.
Cognate with 物(もの) (mono, “thing”, physical as opposed to abstract).
In ancient texts marked with pronunciation information, this character was always read as hito until around the late 800s, at which point the mono reading becomes prevalent. The mono reading has historically often been used with mild pejorative overtones, as compared to the more neutral term 人(ひと) (hito). This may suggest a broadening of the original “thing” sense for mono, which then was applied as a pejorative for a “person”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/mono/ → /mon/
Shift from mono above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 者 (MC tsyaeX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
裏(うら) (ura, “back”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “opening, door”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Cognate with 攻(せ)める (semeru), 責(せ)める (semeru), 狭(せば)める (sebameru), 狭(せば)まる (sebamaru), and 狭(せま)い (semai).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Extended from the “to approach” sense of 迫(せま)る (semaru) above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appeared in the book on physics 気海観瀾 (Kikai Kanran) of 1827. Until the end of the Edo period, the term was used as a translation of Dutch lucht (“air”). In the early Meiji period, it became common as a translation of English atmosphere, and in the late Meiji period, it changed to an abstract meaning as it is today.
